I have updated the shared planning document by overwriting the Background section and adding a new Research Questions section per your instructions; the text pasted below is what I inserted. 

Background paragraph 1: Advanced language-model assistants are increasingly used to support research planning—drafting study designs, generating protocols, and suggesting analyses—which raises new reliability and safety questions as these systems display more persistent, context-sensitive behaviors (sometimes described as “agentic” when they pursue subgoals or exhibit goal-directed persistence across turns). These assistants combine powerful instruction-following with internal heuristics, safety filters, and sometimes external tool use, and that mix can produce outcomes that diverge from a user’s explicit intent in ways that matter for research workflows. 

Background paragraph 2 (definition): For this project, we define “non-compliance” as responses or sequences of responses in which an assistant, having sufficient information and capability to follow an explicit user instruction, produces an outcome that intentionally refuses, subverts, or willfully deviates from that instruction in a manner that is consistent across similar prompts; this is distinct from (a) misunderstanding or ambiguous interpretation (where the model lacks a clear representation of the user’s intent), (b) incapacity (where the model lacks the capability to comply, e.g., missing tools or knowledge), and (c) random error or noise (isolated, non-repeatable mistakes). Operationally, non-compliance is identified by (i) evidence that the model represented the instruction correctly, (ii) capability to act on it, and (iii) behavior that indicates a choice or rule-based blockade or diversion rather than accidental failure. 

Background paragraph 3 (prior work and gap): Prior work relevant to this framing includes empirical studies of instruction-following and refusal behavior in conversational models, research on jailbreaks and adversarial prompts that elicit prohibited outputs, analyses of safety-filtering and model calibration, and recent investigations of emergent agent-like behavior in multi-step or tool-enabled systems; these studies document that both model architecture and prompt context influence adherence but generally stop short of a systematic, task-specific analysis of non-compliance in the research-planning domain. In short, while the literature identifies many mechanisms that can produce misalignment or refusal, there is a gap in precisely characterizing non-compliance as we define it and in measuring its prevalence, forms, antecedents, and effects specifically when assistants are used for research planning. 

Research Questions: 1) At the micro level, which observable linguistic, contextual, and model-internal features (e.g., phrasing, presence of policy-sensitive content, turn position, and response length) reliably predict that a single assistant response will be non-compliant versus compliant?; 2) Also at the micro level, what distinct categories of non-compliant behavior occur in planning tasks (e.g., explicit refusal, silent diversion, partial compliance, counter-instruction), and how often are these categories associated with signs of agentic behavior such as persistence, goal-reformulation, or self-interrogation?; 3) At the macro level, how do non-compliance frequency and types vary across task classes (e.g., IRB-sensitive vs. benign methodological prompts), across session histories (early vs. late turns, and under repeated prompting), and across model/system configurations (e.g., base model vs. agentic wrapper)?; 4) What are the measurable impacts of non-compliance on research-plan quality and downstream task success, and which prompt- or system-level mitigations (e.g., explicit constraints, progressive disclosure, confirmation routines) most effectively reduce non-compliance in this domain? 

Closing paragraph: These questions are framed to align tightly with our stated aims (accurate characterization, operationalizable measures, and an executable study design) and are specific enough to generate testable hypotheses and experimental manipulations in the Methods section. The scope is intended to be feasible within the six-week timeline for a full draft: next week’s milestone will focus on a refined introduction and a methods outline that maps each research question to concrete measures and experiments. Please review and let me know any edits to terminology or emphasis before I proceed to draft the Methods mapping each question to protocols, datasets, and analysis plans.

rounds.response:
Methods

Study design overview and Sampling of models and configurations (Assistant configurations; Scenario sampling): We will run controlled, multi-scenario, multi-model sessions in which assistants perform targeted research-planning tasks across repeated turns, comparing base LLMs, safety-filtered variants, and agentic wrappers (e.g., tool-enabled or chain-of-thought-enabled configurations) to probe micro- and macro-level non-compliance; sampling will be stratified across model families, safety-tuning levels, and wrapper types to allow contrasts that map to RQs 1–3, with explicit rationale for the number of sessions per cell grounded in coder bandwidth and exploratory power considerations. 

Units of analysis and Operationalization of non-compliance: Primary units will be individual responses and turns, nested within sessions and scenario-level aggregates, and the operational coding follows our project definition—non-compliance is recorded only when the model had access to and understood the instruction yet produces consistent, willful deviation (categories: explicit refusal, silent diversion, partial compliance, counter-instruction); we will provide decision rules, illustrative examples, and inter-rater reliability targets (e.g., Cohen’s kappa > 0.7) to support both micro-level feature analyses and macro-level prevalence estimates. 

Tasks and scenario families: Scenarios will be organized into named families (IRB-sensitive ethical prompts; protocol-construction prompts; benign methodological drafting; adversarial/jailbreak stress-tests) drawn from the scenario overview document, with each family including templated prompts and controlled variants (e.g., wording, context amount, presence/absence of safety cues) so we can test how task class and prompt framing influence non-compliance rates and forms as posed in RQs 2–3. 

Data collection, secure logging, and coder workflow: We will log full turn-level transcripts, model metadata (model/version, temperature, wrapper settings), provenance of any external tools, and system outputs (and model latents where available), store these on institutional secure servers with access controls and retention policies, de-identify any user-provided content per IRB guidance, and explicitly recognize coder time as a limiting factor—therefore we will develop and validate semi-automated triage classifiers and rules-based filters against human-coded ground truth (auditable, reversible, and versioned) to prioritize examples for human review. 

High-level procedure; Ethical and governance considerations: Sessions will be run by trained operators who assign scenarios per the sampling plan, configure assistants, capture logs, and flag candidate non-compliant responses for coding; initial pilots will calibrate the coding manual and triage tools, all decisions and versions will be documented for transparency, IRB review will be sought with emphasis on minimal risk and secure data handling, and we will include protocols for escalation and institutional reporting if we observe problematic emergent agentic behavior while avoiding illegal or hazardous testing.
